title: Prevalence of Schistosoma mansoni Infection Among Children in Ethiopia: Epidemiological Patterns, Determinants, and Evidence Synthesis

subsections.section_title: Epidemiological and Public Health Context of Schistosoma mansoni in Ethiopia
subsections.subsection_title: Biology and Transmission of Schistosoma mansoni
subsections.content:
Schistosoma mansoni is a dioecious trematode responsible for intestinal schistosomiasis in humans. Adult worms inhabit the mesenteric venules, where paired females deposit eggs; a proportion of these traverse the intestinal wall and are excreted in feces, while many are retained in host tissues and drive granulomatous inflammation, periportal fibrosis, and chronic morbidity. Thus, pathology arises largely from the host immune response to deposited eggs rather than from the presence of adult worms alone ref [1].

Transmission depends on a freshwater snail intermediate host, principally Biomphalaria spp. Eggs reaching water hatch into miracidia that infect suitable snails, within which asexual multiplication produces cercariae. These free-swimming cercariae are released into freshwater and penetrate human skin during contact with contaminated rivers, lakes, ponds, canals, or irrigation schemes. The life cycle therefore links human contamination of water sources with repeated water exposure, making transmission highly sensitive to sanitation, snail habitat ecology, and patterns of occupational and domestic water use ref [2].

In endemic settings such as Ethiopia, this biology helps explain the focal yet persistent distribution of S. mansoni. School-age children are especially exposed because of frequent bathing, swimming, laundry assistance, and play in infested water, while poor sanitation sustains environmental seeding of eggs. The compatibility between parasite, snail host, and local freshwater environments underpins marked micro-geographic variation in prevalence and intensity, even across neighboring communities.

subsections.section_title: Epidemiological and Public Health Context of Schistosoma mansoni in Ethiopia
subsections.subsection_title: Burden of Intestinal Schistosomiasis in Sub-Saharan Africa
subsections.content:
Intestinal schistosomiasis remains one of the most important helminthic diseases in sub-Saharan Africa, where Schistosoma mansoni is sustained by extensive human-water contact, inadequate sanitation, and the wide distribution of compatible Biomphalaria snail hosts. Regional burden estimates have consistently shown that Africa carries the overwhelming majority of global schistosomiasis cases, with school-age children bearing a disproportionate share of infection intensity and morbidity because of frequent exposure during bathing, swimming, and domestic water collection activities [1].

Beyond infection counts, the burden of S. mansoni in the region is expressed through chronic anemia, undernutrition, reduced physical fitness, impaired cognition and school performance, and progressive hepatointestinal disease in heavily exposed communities. Mapping and geostatistical analyses have further demonstrated that transmission is highly focal, clustering around lakes, irrigation systems, and river basins, which creates substantial within-country heterogeneity and complicates control planning [2]. This broader sub-Saharan African pattern is directly relevant to Ethiopia, where localized ecological suitability and unequal access to water, sanitation, and preventive chemotherapy shape marked variation in prevalence among children.

The persistence of intestinal schistosomiasis in sub-Saharan Africa also reflects structural challenges in control programs. Although preventive chemotherapy has expanded considerably, reinfection remains common where treatment is not paired with improved sanitation, safe water access, and snail habitat management. As a result, the regional burden should be understood not only as a parasitological problem but also as a marker of entrenched environmental and social inequities.

subsections.section_title: Epidemiological and Public Health Context of Schistosoma mansoni in Ethiopia
subsections.content:
Children bear a disproportionate share of Schistosoma mansoni infection because their daily activities frequently involve contact with cercariae-infested water during bathing, swimming, laundry assistance, and water collection. In endemic settings, repeated exposure begins early in life and often coincides with limited acquired immunity, poor sanitation, and constrained access to diagnosis and treatment. School-age children therefore tend to show the highest infection intensities, making them the principal target group for preventive chemotherapy and morbidity control programs ref [4].

The consequences of chronic intestinal schistosomiasis in childhood extend beyond acute gastrointestinal symptoms. Persistent egg deposition and inflammatory responses can contribute to iron-deficiency anemia, undernutrition, impaired linear growth, reduced physical fitness, and diminished educational performance through absenteeism and poorer cognitive function. At higher intensities, hepatosplenic morbidity and periportal fibrosis may emerge over time, underscoring that childhood infection is not a transient parasitic event but part of a cumulative disease process with life-course implications ref [1].

In Ethiopia, these vulnerabilities are amplified by rural dependence on open freshwater bodies, uneven water and sanitation infrastructure, and ecological conditions favorable to transmission. As a result, childhood schistosomiasis must be understood not only as an infection of high prevalence, but also as a developmental and public health problem that intersects with nutrition, schooling, and long-term productivity.

subsections.section_title: Epidemiological and Public Health Context of Schistosoma mansoni in Ethiopia
subsections.subsection_title: Ecological and Geographic Features of Ethiopia
subsections.content:
Ethiopia’s ecological heterogeneity is central to the epidemiology of Schistosoma mansoni. Marked variation in altitude, temperature, rainfall, and hydrology creates sharply contrasting transmission settings, from humid lake and river basins to cooler highland zones where transmission is limited or absent. This environmental diversity shapes the distribution of Biomphalaria intermediate host snails and helps explain the focal nature of intestinal schistosomiasis across the country ref [5].

Transmission is especially associated with perennial and seasonal freshwater bodies, including lakes, irrigation canals, streams, dams, and marshy habitats that support human water contact for bathing, washing, fishing, and agriculture. Large water-resource developments have also altered local ecology by expanding snail habitats and increasing human exposure opportunities. National geospatial analyses have shown that Ethiopian schistosomiasis risk clusters along suitable climatic and hydrological corridors rather than being uniformly distributed, reinforcing the importance of local environmental conditions in determining endemicity ref [6].

These geographic features have practical implications for surveillance and control. Because transmission is highly focal, prevalence among children can vary substantially between nearby communities depending on proximity to infected water bodies, sanitation coverage, and patterns of livelihood-related contact. In Ethiopia, ecological setting therefore provides an essential framework for interpreting prevalence estimates and for targeting school-based treatment, snail control, and water, sanitation, and hygiene interventions.

subsections.section_title: Epidemiological and Public Health Context of Schistosoma mansoni in Ethiopia
subsections.subsection_title: Schistosomiasis within Ethiopia’s Neglected Tropical Disease Agenda
subsections.content:
Within Ethiopia’s neglected tropical disease (NTD) agenda, schistosomiasis is prioritized as a major helminth infection because of its contribution to chronic morbidity, its overlap with poverty and poor water access, and its concentration among school-age children. National mapping and burden assessments helped establish schistosomiasis as a geographically focal but substantial public health problem, supporting its inclusion alongside soil-transmitted helminthiases in large-scale preventive chemotherapy and control planning ref [7].

Ethiopia’s policy response has increasingly aligned schistosomiasis control with integrated NTD delivery platforms, particularly school-based deworming, district-level risk stratification, and coordinated monitoring of co-endemic helminth infections. This integrated approach reflects evidence that the country carries a large burden of both schistosomiasis and soil-transmitted helminths, making combined treatment strategies operationally efficient and epidemiologically justified ref [8].

At the same time, Ethiopia’s NTD agenda has moved beyond chemotherapy alone toward transmission interruption concepts that emphasize water, sanitation, hygiene, and local ecological surveillance. For Schistosoma mansoni, this is especially important because persistent transmission in lake, river, and irrigation settings can sustain reinfection despite repeated mass drug administration. Consequently, schistosomiasis occupies a strategic place in Ethiopian NTD programming as both a disease of immediate child health importance and a marker of broader environmental inequity.

subsections.section_title: Patterns of Prevalence and Distribution Among Children in Ethiopia
subsections.content:
At the national level, available evidence indicates that Schistosoma mansoni remains a substantial parasitic infection among Ethiopian children, but reported prevalence estimates vary widely because studies are concentrated in ecologically favorable transmission zones rather than being uniformly representative of the country. National syntheses therefore suggest a considerable overall burden while also warning that pooled estimates should be interpreted as summaries of heterogeneous local epidemics rather than a single stable national rate ref [9].

This broad national picture is consistent with large-scale mapping and school-age risk assessments showing that intestinal schistosomiasis is distributed in focal patterns linked to freshwater exposure, altitude, sanitation conditions, and the presence of intermediate host snails. In practical terms, the national overview is one of moderate-to-high burden in many child populations, with marked clustering in endemic districts and lower prevalence in non-suitable ecological areas, underscoring the need to read national averages alongside subnational stratification ref [10].

Accordingly, national prevalence estimates are most useful as programmatic indicators for prioritization, drug procurement, and broad burden assessment, but they do not eliminate the need for district- and community-level surveillance. For Ethiopian children, the central message from the literature is that S. mansoni remains widely established, yet its apparent national prevalence is strongly shaped by where surveys are conducted and which child populations are sampled ref [9], ref [10].

subsections.section_title: Patterns of Prevalence and Distribution Among Children in Ethiopia
subsections.content:
A consistent feature of Schistosoma mansoni epidemiology in Ethiopian children is marked regional and even micro-local heterogeneity. Prevalence is typically concentrated in settings with suitable Biomphalaria habitats and frequent human water contact, especially communities located near lakes, rivers, streams, irrigation canals, and dams. This produces sharp contrasts not only between regions but also between neighboring districts and schools, so that national or regional averages often obscure localized transmission hotspots.

Evidence from school-based investigations illustrates this patchiness. In northern Ethiopia, very high infection levels have been documented among children in communities associated with stream- and irrigation-linked transmission, while other nearby settings report far lower burdens, underscoring the focal character of exposure and parasite maintenance ref [11]. Comparable spatial clustering has also been observed in multivillage studies from southern Ethiopia, where schistosomiasis risk varied strongly with proximity to infested water bodies and local ecological conditions rather than broad administrative boundaries alone ref [12].

For interpretation of pooled prevalence estimates, this heterogeneity has two implications. First, between-study variation in Ethiopian pediatric surveys is likely to reflect real ecological and behavioral differences, not merely methodological inconsistency. Second, control strategies should prioritize sub-regional mapping and hotspot-oriented delivery of praziquantel, snail control, and water, sanitation, and hygiene measures, since transmission intensity can differ substantially over short geographic distances.

subsections.section_title: Patterns of Prevalence and Distribution Among Children in Ethiopia
subsections.content:
Age-specific analyses of Schistosoma mansoni infection among Ethiopian children generally show a rise in prevalence through late childhood, often peaking in the 10–14 year age range. This pattern is consistent with the broader epidemiology of intestinal schistosomiasis, in which cumulative water contact and growing mobility increase exposure during school-age years, while infection in younger children is increasingly recognized where domestic or recreational contact with infested water begins early. Evidence from national mapping and school-based surveys in Ethiopia has repeatedly identified school-age children as the core high-risk group for preventive chemotherapy and surveillance ref [13], ref [14].

Sex-specific differences are less uniform than age effects but many Ethiopian studies report higher prevalence or heavier infection among boys. The usual explanation is behavioral rather than biological: boys may spend more time swimming, herding animals, fishing, or crossing streams, leading to more frequent cercarial exposure. However, sex gaps are not universal, and in some settings girls show comparable infection levels where water collection, laundering, and other domestic activities produce similar contact patterns. This implies that sex differentials should be interpreted in relation to local livelihoods and gendered roles rather than assumed to be fixed across endemic areas ref [14], ref [2].

Taken together, the Ethiopian literature suggests that age is the more consistent axis of stratification, whereas sex patterns are context dependent. For control planning, this supports prioritization of school-age children while also recognizing that both younger children and girls may be substantially exposed in communities with intense transmission and daily reliance on unsafe freshwater sources.

subsections.section_title: Patterns of Prevalence and Distribution Among Children in Ethiopia
subsections.content:
In Ethiopia, much of the evidence on Schistosoma mansoni among children comes from school-based surveys because schools provide efficient access to large numbers of children and have been central to mapping for preventive chemotherapy. These studies are highly informative for identifying transmission foci, but they do not necessarily represent all children at risk. Enrollment is uneven across rural settings, and non-enrolled children may differ systematically in water contact, sanitation, and treatment access; consequently, school-derived prevalence can either under- or overestimate community burden depending on local social and ecological conditions ref [15].

Community-based studies, by contrast, capture pre-school children, non-attenders, and out-of-school adolescents, thereby offering a broader picture of infection distribution. This distinction matters in Ethiopia because transmission is strongly linked to proximity to infested water bodies and livelihood-related exposure, factors that are not fully captured by school sampling frames. National mapping and burden assessments in sub-Saharan Africa have therefore emphasized that school-aged children are useful sentinels for control, but that extrapolation from school surveys to the wider community should be made cautiously, especially in heterogeneous endemic settings ref [16].

Taken together, Ethiopian findings should be interpreted with attention to sampling platform. School-based data are often most suitable for programmatic targeting and trend monitoring in the main at-risk age group, whereas community-based data are more appropriate for estimating population-wide burden and identifying neglected reservoirs of infection among children excluded from school-centered interventions.

subsections.section_title: Patterns of Prevalence and Distribution Among Children in Ethiopia
subsections.content:
Temporal interpretation of Schistosoma mansoni burden among Ethiopian children requires caution because apparent changes over time reflect both true epidemiologic shifts and changes in study design, diagnostic method, and intervention coverage. Nevertheless, the literature suggests that transmission has remained persistently important in many endemic foci over several decades, with marked local declines in some school-aged populations after preventive chemotherapy and continued high prevalence in communities where water contact and sanitation conditions remain favorable for transmission.

Nationally, the expansion of school-based deworming and mapping activities after the 2010s created a more coherent picture of burden and helped identify districts requiring repeated praziquantel distribution. The Ethiopian national mapping of schistosomiasis and soil-transmitted helminthiasis showed that substantial pediatric risk persisted across many districts even in the period of scaled control, underscoring that temporal reductions have been uneven rather than universal ref [17]. This pattern is consistent with broader African analyses showing that chemotherapy can reduce prevalence and especially heavy-intensity infection, but that rebound or residual transmission is common where treatment is not complemented by improvements in water, sanitation, hygiene, and snail-control measures ref [18].

Accordingly, temporal trends in Ethiopia are best understood as heterogeneous trajectories: modest to substantial declines in some treated school settings, relative stability in others, and continued focal transmission in ecologically suitable areas. For survey interpretation, this means that older prevalence estimates should not simply be pooled with newer studies without accounting for intervention era, surveillance intensity, and diagnostic sensitivity.

subsections.section_title: Patterns of Prevalence and Distribution Among Children in Ethiopia
subsections.subsection_title: Intensity of Infection and Clinical Relevance
subsections.content:
Beyond point prevalence, infection intensity is critical for interpreting the burden of Schistosoma mansoni among Ethiopian children because morbidity is more closely related to worm burden than to infection status alone. Surveys in Ethiopia commonly classify intensity by eggs per gram of stool using WHO thresholds, and many settings report predominantly light-to-moderate infections alongside smaller but epidemiologically important pockets of heavy infection. This distinction matters because average prevalence can obscure communities in which a minority of heavily infected children sustain transmission and face disproportionate health risks.

The clinical relevance of intensity is substantial in school-age children. Higher egg counts are associated with hepatointestinal morbidity, including diarrhoea, blood loss, undernutrition, impaired physical fitness, and later hepatosplenic complications, while even moderate infections can contribute to anaemia and reduced well-being when they occur repeatedly or alongside other parasitic diseases ref [19], ref [1]. In endemic African settings, the heaviest burdens typically cluster in children of school age, reinforcing why this age group remains the main target of preventive chemotherapy and morbidity control.

For Ethiopian epidemiology, intensity data therefore add an essential layer to prevalence mapping. They help distinguish low-prevalence areas with limited morbidity from transmission foci where heavy infections persist despite apparently modest overall prevalence, and they are particularly useful for evaluating programme impact after praziquantel distribution. Accordingly, interpretation of regional patterns should consider both how many children are infected and how intensely they are infected.

subsections.section_title: Determinants and Risk Factors Associated with Infection in Children
subsections.content:
Water contact behavior is one of the most proximate determinants of Schistosoma mansoni acquisition in children because transmission depends on repeated skin exposure to cercariae-infested freshwater. In Ethiopian settings, the highest-risk activities are typically swimming, bathing, playing, washing clothes, fetching water, and crossing streams or irrigation canals barefoot, all of which increase both frequency and duration of exposure. School-age children are especially vulnerable because recreational water play and routine domestic assistance often coincide with peak contact with rivers, ponds, and canals.

Evidence from Ethiopian field studies shows that children reporting swimming or frequent river contact consistently have higher odds of intestinal schistosomiasis than those with limited exposure. In northern Ethiopia, Alemayehu and Tomass documented marked associations between swimming, bathing, and washing clothes in rivers and S. mansoni infection among schoolchildren, underscoring the importance of repeated contact for transmission ref [20]. Similar patterns have been reported from other endemic Ethiopian localities, where water-related recreation and household chores structure age- and sex-specific risk profiles ref [21].

These behavioral pathways also interact with local ecology and infrastructure. Where safe water access is limited, children may rely on open freshwater for daily needs, making exposure difficult to avoid even when awareness of infection exists. Thus, water contact behavior should be interpreted not merely as an individual choice but as a socially patterned exposure shaped by labor roles, seasonality, and the availability of alternative water sources.

subsections.section_title: Determinants and Risk Factors Associated with Infection in Children
subsections.content:
Sanitation and hygiene shape children’s risk of Schistosoma mansoni infection by influencing the degree to which human fecal contamination reaches transmission sites. In endemic settings, open defecation near streams, ponds, irrigation channels, or lakes can sustain the parasite’s life cycle by introducing eggs into freshwater where Biomphalaria snails occur. Conversely, access to and consistent use of latrines may reduce environmental seeding, although the protective effect is often partial when sanitation coverage is incomplete or when children continue to defecate outdoors during school or field activities. Ethiopian studies of school-age children have repeatedly identified poor sanitation conditions and limited hygiene-related knowledge or practice as correlates of infection or higher prevalence clusters ref [22], ref [23].

From a transmission perspective, hygiene should be interpreted primarily through its relationship to exposure ecology rather than as an isolated household behavior. Handwashing and general cleanliness are important for overall child health, but for intestinal schistosomiasis they are less decisive than the sanitary containment of feces and the contamination status of nearby water bodies. This helps explain why communities with modest household sanitation improvements may still experience persistent transmission when shared water contact points remain contaminated and when schools lack adequate latrine infrastructure. Broader syntheses of schistosomiasis control therefore emphasize sanitation as a complementary, but not stand-alone, intervention alongside chemotherapy and reduced contact with unsafe water ref [24].

subsections.section_title: Determinants and Risk Factors Associated with Infection in Children
subsections.subsection_title: Proximity to Freshwater Sources and Snail Habitats
subsections.content:
Proximity to lakes, rivers, irrigation canals, and other perennial freshwater bodies is a consistent spatial determinant of Schistosoma mansoni transmission because it shapes the frequency and intensity of children’s contact with cercariae-infested water. In Ethiopian settings, communities located near Lake Tana and other water bodies have repeatedly shown higher infection burdens, reflecting the close linkage between settlement patterns, routine water use, and transmission ecology ref [25]. Distance is therefore not simply a geographic measure; it proxies ease of access to unsafe water for bathing, playing, washing, and crossing streams during daily activities.

Risk is further amplified when nearby water bodies support Biomphalaria snail populations, the intermediate hosts required for S. mansoni transmission. Ethiopian malacological studies have documented infected Biomphalaria pfeifferi in human-water-contact sites, demonstrating that the presence of suitable snail habitats can convert ordinary freshwater access points into active transmission foci ref [26]. Slow-flowing shorelines, irrigation margins, vegetated pools, and seasonal stagnation zones are especially important because they sustain snail breeding and increase the likelihood that children encounter contaminated water during recreation or domestic chores.

Accordingly, heterogeneity in child infection risk across Ethiopia should be interpreted in ecological as well as behavioral terms. Even where water contact is common, transmission tends to cluster around settlements adjacent to suitable snail habitats, while more distant households may face lower cumulative exposure. This spatial perspective is important for targeting school-based treatment, snail surveillance, and environmental interventions toward communities living closest to persistent transmission sites.

subsections.section_title: Determinants and Risk Factors Associated with Infection in Children
subsections.content:
Socioeconomic and household-level conditions shape children’s exposure to Schistosoma mansoni by influencing where families live, how water is obtained, and the extent to which households can avoid frequent contact with unsafe surface water. In Ethiopian settings, lower household wealth is often associated with dependence on unimproved water sources, limited sanitation, and residence in environmentally marginal areas near transmission sites, thereby increasing repeated exposure among school-age children. Household crowding and constrained parental resources may also reduce supervision and limit the ability to adopt preventive practices, even where infection awareness exists.

Evidence from Ethiopian school-based epidemiology indicates that markers of household disadvantage, including low parental education and poorer living conditions, are recurrently associated with higher odds of intestinal schistosomiasis, although effect sizes vary by locality and study design ref [27]. Broader analyses of schistosomiasis and soil-transmitted helminth co-distribution in Ethiopia similarly suggest that social vulnerability and service deprivation help structure infection risk across communities, interacting with ecological suitability rather than operating independently ref [28].

These patterns imply that socioeconomic status should be understood as a distal determinant that works through proximal pathways such as water contact, sanitation access, treatment uptake, and residential location. For interpretation of prevalence heterogeneity in Ethiopian children, household-level indicators are therefore most informative when analyzed together with environmental exposure and school- or community-level conditions rather than as isolated covariates.

subsections.section_title: Determinants and Risk Factors Associated with Infection in Children
subsections.subsection_title: Schooling, Occupation, and Daily Activity Patterns
subsections.content:
Schooling, household occupation, and children’s routine activity patterns shape exposure opportunities to Schistosoma mansoni by determining how often and for what purposes children contact cercariae-infested water. In Ethiopian settings, infection has often been concentrated in school-age children, partly because this age group combines high mobility and autonomy with frequent recreational swimming, bathing, and water fetching before and after school. School-based parasitological surveys from northwest Ethiopia have linked swimming and repeated river contact with higher odds of S. mansoni infection, illustrating how daily schedules around school attendance can still sustain substantial exposure when freshwater use remains integral to household life ref [29].

Occupation-related risk operates largely through family livelihood systems. Children from farming, fishing, irrigation, or other water-dependent households may accompany adults to rivers, canals, ponds, or lakeshores, or assume domestic labor roles such as laundering animals, washing clothes, or collecting water. These patterns can increase both frequency and duration of exposure, especially where safe water alternatives are unavailable. Evidence from studies in Ethiopia and elsewhere indicates that water-contact intensity, rather than schooling alone, is the more proximate determinant, with boys often showing higher prevalence because gendered daily activities more commonly involve swimming, herding, or outdoor tasks near transmission sites ref [30].

Accordingly, schooling should be interpreted not simply as a protective social determinant, but as a factor interacting with children’s time use, gender norms, and household labor demands. Risk reduction in Ethiopian schoolchildren is therefore likely to depend on interventions that extend beyond classroom-based health education to include safer water access, behaviorally informed scheduling of water-related chores, and targeting of high-exposure occupational and after-school routines.

subsections.section_title: Determinants and Risk Factors Associated with Infection in Children
subsections.subsection_title: Co-endemicity and Nutritional or Health Status
subsections.content:
In Ethiopian children, risk and consequences of S. mansoni infection are often shaped by co-endemic parasitic and nutritional conditions rather than by schistosomiasis alone. Polyparasitism is common in many endemic settings, particularly where schistosomiasis overlaps with soil-transmitted helminths and malaria, and this clustering can amplify morbidity through shared environmental exposures and cumulative effects on anemia, growth, and school performance. Evidence from school-age populations in sub-Saharan Africa has shown that concurrent helminth infections are frequent and epidemiologically patterned, indicating that observed infection risk should be interpreted within a broader syndemic context rather than as an isolated exposure outcome [1].

Nutritional and general health status may also influence both susceptibility and clinical expression. Chronic undernutrition, iron deficiency, and recurrent infectious disease can interact with intestinal schistosomiasis to worsen anemia and physical debility, while heavily infected children may experience appetite loss, inflammation, and impaired growth. In turn, poor baseline nutritional status may heighten vulnerability to the functional consequences of infection even when parasite intensity is moderate. Broader analyses of schistosomiasis-associated morbidity in children support this bidirectional relationship, linking infection with anemia, undernutrition, and reduced well-being, particularly where multiple deprivation factors coexist [2].

For Ethiopian epidemiological studies, these interactions imply that variation in prevalence and morbidity between communities may partly reflect differences in background malaria transmission, intestinal helminth burden, and food insecurity. Risk-factor models that omit co-endemic infections or nutritional indicators may therefore underestimate the social and biological determinants of infection and obscure which children face the greatest cumulative burden.

subsections.section_title: Diagnostic Approaches and Measurement Challenges in Prevalence Studies
subsections.content:
Parasitological diagnosis has historically been the cornerstone of prevalence studies of Schistosoma mansoni in children because it detects parasite eggs directly in stool and can provide semi-quantitative information on infection intensity. The Kato-Katz thick smear remains the most widely used field method owing to its low cost, simplicity, and compatibility with epidemiologic surveys, especially in school-based settings. Standardized procedures for preparation and egg counting enabled its broad adoption in control programs and research, making it the dominant basis for cross-study prevalence comparisons despite known limitations at low infection intensity ref [33].

Alternative parasitological methods have been used to address some of these constraints. Formol-ether or formalin-ethyl acetate concentration techniques and related stool concentration methods can improve egg recovery in some settings, while hatching-based procedures such as the miracidium hatching test have also been applied, particularly where confirmation of active infection is important. However, these methods are generally more labor-intensive, less standardized across surveys, or operationally less feasible for large pediatric prevalence studies than Kato-Katz. Consequently, the choice of parasitological method introduces important heterogeneity, since diagnostic yield depends not only on the assay itself but also on stool quantity, timing of slide reading, and technician expertise ref [34].

In prevalence syntheses, these methodological differences matter because parasitological tools do not measure a fixed underlying construct with equal efficiency across transmission settings. Surveys based on a single Kato-Katz smear may systematically miss light infections, whereas studies using duplicate smears, multiple stools, or concentration methods may report higher prevalence under otherwise similar epidemiologic conditions. Careful attention to the specific parasitological protocol is therefore essential when interpreting between-study variation in estimated S. mansoni burden among children.

subsections.section_title: Diagnostic Approaches and Measurement Challenges in Prevalence Studies
subsections.content:
Differences in sensitivity and specificity are central to explaining heterogeneity in reported Schistosoma mansoni prevalence among children. Egg-detection methods such as Kato-Katz are highly specific because visualized eggs provide direct parasitological confirmation, but sensitivity declines sharply in light-intensity infections and when only a single stool specimen or few smears are examined. This means that studies conducted after repeated mass drug administration, or in lower-transmission settings, may substantially underestimate true prevalence if they rely on limited microscopy alone ref [35].

By contrast, antigen-detection approaches, particularly point-of-care circulating cathodic antigen (POC-CCA), generally show higher sensitivity than single- or duplicate-slide Kato-Katz for intestinal schistosomiasis, especially where infection intensity is low. However, this gain in sensitivity may be accompanied by reduced specificity or interpretive ambiguity around trace-positive results, which can shift estimated prevalence upward relative to stool microscopy. Comparative evaluations therefore indicate that apparent between-study differences may reflect diagnostic performance rather than true epidemiologic variation ref [36].

For prevalence synthesis, diagnostic performance should not be treated as a fixed property of a test, but as context dependent: it varies with infection intensity, sampling effort, age distribution, and reference standard assumptions. Consequently, pooled estimates that combine studies using different diagnostic platforms without adjustment risk conflating measurement error with biological variation.

subsections.section_title: Diagnostic Approaches and Measurement Challenges in Prevalence Studies
subsections.content:
Whether prevalence is estimated from a single stool specimen or from repeated specimens collected on consecutive days is a major determinant of measured Schistosoma mansoni burden in children. Egg excretion fluctuates from day to day and within the same day, so reliance on one specimen, particularly when only one or two Kato-Katz thick smears are examined, systematically misses low-intensity infections and produces downwardly biased prevalence estimates. This problem becomes more pronounced in low-transmission settings and after preventive chemotherapy, when infections are lighter and more heterogeneous.

Empirical studies have shown that examining multiple stool samples substantially improves case detection relative to a single-sample strategy. In field evaluations, repeated Kato-Katz sampling increased observed prevalence and altered infection-intensity classifications, demonstrating that part of the between-study variation in prevalence reflects sampling design rather than true epidemiologic differences ref [37]. Similar conclusions were reinforced in comparative diagnostic work showing that day-to-day replication raises the sensitivity of stool microscopy, although gains diminish with each additional specimen and must be balanced against cost, participant burden, and logistical complexity ref [38].

For comparative synthesis, studies using single-sample designs should therefore not be treated as methodologically equivalent to those using repeated sampling. At minimum, meta-analytic interpretation should consider the number of stools collected, the number of smears prepared per stool, and the timing of collection, because these design choices affect both absolute prevalence and apparent programmatic progress.

subsections.section_title: Diagnostic Approaches and Measurement Challenges in Prevalence Studies
subsections.subsection_title: Case Definitions and Thresholds for Infection
subsections.content:
Case definitions for Schistosoma mansoni infection are not uniform across prevalence studies, and this lack of standardization can materially alter reported burden. Many surveys define infection as the detection of at least one egg on Kato–Katz thick smear, whereas others classify cases using point-of-care circulating cathodic antigen positivity, PCR detection, or composite definitions that combine parasitological and antigen-based results. Because these approaches capture different biological targets and have different limits of detection, apparently similar prevalence estimates may not be directly comparable, especially in low-intensity settings where egg excretion is intermittent and many infections fall below microscopy thresholds ref [39].

Thresholds used to categorize infection intensity introduce an additional layer of heterogeneity. WHO guidance has long operationalized S. mansoni intensity using eggs per gram of feces, typically distinguishing light (1–99 epg), moderate (100–399 epg), and heavy (>=400 epg) infection; these categories are important because morbidity risk, treatment priorities, and programmatic classification often rely on them rather than on infection status alone ref [40]. However, intensity classes derived from a small number of stool samples are sensitive to day-to-day variation in egg output, so misclassification between light and moderate infection is common.

For comparative synthesis, prevalence reviews should therefore extract not only the diagnostic method but also the exact case definition, positivity threshold, and intensity cut-points applied. Distinguishing egg-patent infection from antigen-detected infection is particularly important when pooling studies across transmission settings or over time, since control programs can reduce intensity before eliminating infection, thereby changing the relationship between diagnostic positivity and clinically meaningful disease.

subsections.section_title: Diagnostic Approaches and Measurement Challenges in Prevalence Studies
subsections.subsection_title: Quality Assurance in Laboratory and Field Procedures
subsections.content:
Quality assurance is a major determinant of the reliability of prevalence estimates in school-age children because schistosomiasis diagnostics are highly operator- and workflow-dependent. In Kato-Katz-based surveys, variation in stool quantity loaded onto templates, slide preparation, timing of examination, and microscopist experience can materially alter egg detection, especially for light-intensity infections. Standard operating procedures, refresher training, blinded re-reading of a subset of slides, and documentation of discordant results are therefore essential to reduce inter-observer error and between-survey heterogeneity ref [41].

Field procedures are equally important. In community and school surveys, mislabeling of specimens, delays between collection and processing, poor storage conditions, and incomplete sample capture can introduce systematic bias that is rarely recoverable analytically. This is particularly relevant for hookworm but also affects overall stool quality and laboratory throughput in integrated helminth surveys. WHO bench aids and field manuals emphasize standardized labeling, chain-of-custody procedures, predefined reading windows, and supervisory checks as core safeguards for survey validity ref [42].

For comparative synthesis, studies that report explicit quality-control measures should be interpreted as methodologically stronger than those that provide only the diagnostic name. Extraction of whether duplicate readings, external supervision, or repeat examination of discrepant slides were performed can help explain otherwise unexplained prevalence differences across settings and should be considered in risk-of-bias assessment.

subsections.section_title: Diagnostic Approaches and Measurement Challenges in Prevalence Studies
subsections.subsection_title: Implications of Diagnostic Variability for Comparative Synthesis
subsections.content:
Diagnostic variability is a major source of between-study heterogeneity in syntheses of Schistosoma mansoni prevalence among children. Differences in assay choice, stool sampling intensity, slide replication, and infection thresholds alter the probability of detecting light infections, so apparently divergent prevalence estimates may reflect measurement design rather than true epidemiological differences. This problem is especially acute when Kato-Katz–based surveys are pooled alongside studies using more sensitive antigen-detection methods or repeated sampling strategies, because the underlying estimands are not equivalent.

For comparative synthesis, prevalence estimates should therefore be interpreted as test- and protocol-specific observations rather than directly exchangeable measures of infection burden. Empirical evaluations have shown that standard parasitological approaches underestimate prevalence relative to more sensitive diagnostics in low-intensity settings, and that sensitivity declines as transmission intensity falls ref [43], ref [44]. Meta-analyses should consequently extract detailed diagnostic metadata, consider subgrouping by diagnostic platform and sampling scheme, and use meta-regression or sensitivity analyses to assess whether pooled estimates are robust to diagnostic composition.

Where sufficient data are available, calibration or latent-class approaches may better approximate underlying prevalence than naive pooling of observed positives. At minimum, authors should avoid over-interpreting temporal or geographic contrasts when diagnostic protocols differ across studies, because part of the observed variation may be methodological rather than biological.

subsections.section_title: Systematic Review and Meta-Analytic Approaches to Synthesizing Prevalence Evidence
subsections.content:
The review objective should be specified a priori as estimating the pooled prevalence of Schistosoma mansoni infection among children in Ethiopia and characterizing how prevalence varies by place, period, age group, diagnostic approach, and study setting. For prevalence reviews, this objective is best framed within a condition–context–population structure rather than an intervention-focused PICO model, consistent with methodological guidance for systematic reviews of observational epidemiology ref [45]. Clear specification of the target population is especially important in schistosomiasis research because transmission intensity differs markedly between preschool-aged children, school-aged children, and mixed pediatric samples.

Eligibility criteria should therefore include observational studies reporting primary prevalence data for S. mansoni among children residing in Ethiopia, including cross-sectional surveys, baseline data from cohort studies, and control-arm or pre-intervention data from trials when these permit extraction of numerators and denominators. Studies should define infection using recognized parasitological or antigen-based diagnostic methods and provide sufficient information to compute prevalence. Exclusion criteria should typically cover studies outside Ethiopia, studies focused exclusively on adults, case reports, reviews, qualitative reports, and duplicate datasets; when multiple reports describe the same sample, the most complete or recent dataset should be retained.

The eligibility framework should also prespecify contextual restrictions relevant to prevalence synthesis, including study period, language policy, sampling frame, and minimum reporting standards. These decisions improve transparency and reproducibility and align with current guidance for reporting systematic reviews and for conducting reviews of prevalence studies ref [46], ref [47]. In practice, documenting these criteria in a protocol helps limit post hoc selection decisions and strengthens the interpretability of pooled estimates for child schistosomiasis in Ethiopia.

subsections.section_title: Systematic Review and Meta-Analytic Approaches to Synthesizing Prevalence Evidence
subsections.content:
The literature search should be designed to maximize capture of prevalence studies on Schistosoma mansoni among Ethiopian children while preserving transparency and reproducibility. A structured strategy typically combines controlled vocabulary and free-text terms for the parasite, disease, population, outcome, and setting, applied across biomedical and regional databases such as PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, and Google Scholar, with supplementary hand-searching of reference lists and relevant Ethiopian institutional repositories. Reporting of the search process is best aligned with PRISMA 2020, including explicit documentation of databases searched, date ranges, full search strings, duplicate removal procedures, and reasons for exclusion at each screening stage ref [48].

Study identification should proceed through predefined eligibility criteria and independent title/abstract and full-text screening by at least two reviewers. Because prevalence estimates are often reported in cross-sectional surveys, school-based studies, and community-based parasitological investigations, search filters should avoid unnecessary design restrictions that might reduce sensitivity. In prevalence reviews, comprehensive capture is particularly important because selective retrieval can distort pooled estimates and the apparent distribution of infection across regions and age groups. Methodological guidance for reviews of observational epidemiology also emphasizes duplicate screening, explicit management of multiple reports from the same dataset, and maintenance of an auditable study selection log ref [49].

For this topic, the study identification workflow should additionally record locality, diagnostic method, sampling frame, and survey year during screening, because these characteristics are closely tied to comparability and later subgroup analyses. A PRISMA flow diagram can then summarize the number of records identified, screened, assessed for eligibility, and included in the quantitative synthesis.

subsections.section_title: Systematic Review and Meta-Analytic Approaches to Synthesizing Prevalence Evidence
subsections.content:
Data extraction in prevalence reviews should be standardized, duplicate-performed, and anchored to a prespecified form so that epidemiologic differences across studies can be distinguished from reporting variability. For studies of Schistosoma mansoni among Ethiopian children, the minimum extractable items should include study identification, survey year, region and specific locality, study design, school- or community-based sampling frame, age range, sex composition, sample size, number positive, and the reported or calculable prevalence with its diagnostic denominator. Guidance for prevalence reviews further supports extracting the exact case definition, diagnostic method, and analytic details needed to assess comparability across surveys ref [50].

Because prevalence estimates are highly sensitive to measurement choices, study characteristics should capture the parasitological approach in detail: specimen type, number of stool samples, number of Kato-Katz thick smears or alternative tests, intensity metrics where available, and whether quality control procedures were described. It is also important to record environmental and contextual variables that may explain between-study heterogeneity, such as rural versus urban setting, proximity to water bodies, school enrollment context, and season of data collection. Such variables are frequently used in subgroup analysis and meta-regression in prevalence syntheses, particularly when diagnostic and sampling heterogeneity are substantial ref [51].

For synthesis, extracted data should be organized so that multiple prevalence estimates from a single article are handled transparently, for example by separating estimates by district, age group, or diagnostic stratum while avoiding double counting of participants. When information is incomplete, authors should preferentially derive prevalence from raw numerators and denominators and document assumptions about missing data, mixed-age samples, or overlapping populations. A clear tabulation of study characteristics is therefore not merely descriptive; it provides the basis for assessing transportability, selecting appropriate subgroup structures, and interpreting pooled estimates in light of design and measurement differences.

subsections.section_title: Systematic Review and Meta-Analytic Approaches to Synthesizing Prevalence Evidence
subsections.subsection_title: Quality Assessment and Risk of Bias in Prevalence Studies
subsections.content:
Quality appraisal is essential in prevalence reviews because pooled estimates are highly sensitive to flaws in sampling, case ascertainment, and outcome measurement. For studies of Schistosoma mansoni among Ethiopian children, risk-of-bias assessment should therefore focus on whether the target population was clearly defined, whether sampling frames and recruitment procedures were likely to yield representative school-age or preschool-age populations, and whether non-response or missing data could systematically distort prevalence estimates. Instruments developed specifically for prevalence studies are preferable to generic observational checklists because they explicitly address external validity and measurement error in descriptive epidemiology ref [52], ref [53].

A practical appraisal should examine the diagnostic methods used to detect S. mansoni, including the number of stool samples, number of Kato-Katz thick smears, use of concentration techniques, and consistency of laboratory procedures, since imperfect sensitivity can bias prevalence downward. Additional domains include the adequacy of numerator and denominator reporting, consistency of age-range definitions, and whether surveys accounted for clustering by school or community. In endemic settings, temporal factors such as season, prior mass drug administration, and local water-contact ecology may also influence comparability across studies and should be documented as potential sources of bias rather than treated solely as statistical heterogeneity.

Quality ratings should not be used mechanically to exclude all imperfect studies; instead, they should inform sensitivity analyses, subgroup comparisons, and cautious interpretation of pooled prevalence. For example, separate syntheses can be conducted for studies using more sensitive or repeated parasitological assessment versus single-sample surveys, or for community-based versus school-based samples. This approach preserves evidence breadth while making explicit how study limitations may shape the summary estimate and its policy relevance.

subsections.section_title: Systematic Review and Meta-Analytic Approaches to Synthesizing Prevalence Evidence
subsections.content:
Pooling Schistosoma mansoni prevalence requires methods tailored to binomial data, because raw proportions are bounded between 0 and 1 and their variances depend on the observed prevalence and sample size. In prevalence reviews, a random-effects framework is generally preferable to a fixed-effect model because true infection levels are expected to vary across Ethiopian settings owing to differences in ecology, age structure, diagnostic methods, and transmission intensity. This approach explicitly models both within-study sampling error and between-study heterogeneity, yielding a summary estimate that is interpretable as the average prevalence across a distribution of underlying populations rather than a single common value ref [51].

For statistical implementation, generalized linear mixed models or inverse-variance random-effects models applied after an appropriate transformation are commonly used. Historically, the Freeman-Tukey double-arcsine transformation was adopted to stabilize variances when studies reported very low or very high prevalence, including zero-event studies; however, its interpretability and back-transformation have been questioned. Current guidance increasingly favors modeling the binomial likelihood directly through logit-linked mixed models, or using logit-transformed proportions with careful handling of sparse data, because these approaches better preserve the scale and improve inferential coherence ref [54].

Accordingly, in a meta-analysis of S. mansoni prevalence among children, the pooled estimate should be reported with its 95% confidence interval alongside the chosen modeling assumptions, estimator for between-study variance, and any continuity corrections or transformation procedures. Given the likely heterogeneity of prevalence data, the pooled value should be interpreted as a summary of diverse epidemiologic contexts rather than a precise national constant.

subsections.section_title: Systematic Review and Meta-Analytic Approaches to Synthesizing Prevalence Evidence
subsections.subsection_title: Assessment of Heterogeneity and Subgroup Analysis
subsections.content:
Between-study heterogeneity is expected to be substantial in prevalence meta-analyses of Schistosoma mansoni among Ethiopian children because transmission is highly focal and varies with ecology, water contact patterns, sanitation, diagnostic approach, and study design. Heterogeneity should therefore be quantified rather than treated as a nuisance parameter, typically using Cochran’s Q together with the I2 statistic and an estimate of between-study variance under a random-effects framework. However, interpretation should emphasize clinical and methodological sources of inconsistency, since very high I2 values are common in single-arm prevalence syntheses even when studies are all estimating the same broad construct ref [55].

Subgroup analysis is useful for exploring prespecified effect modifiers that are epidemiologically plausible in the Ethiopian setting. Relevant strata include region, study period, rural versus urban setting, age group, sex composition, school-based versus community-based sampling, diagnostic method, and study quality. Because prevalence estimates are bounded and often skewed, analyses should be performed on an appropriate transformed scale and then back-transformed for interpretation. Where enough studies are available, subgroup differences may be supplemented by meta-regression to assess whether observed variation is associated with covariates such as survey year or diagnostic sensitivity, while recognizing the ecological and observational nature of these comparisons ref [51].

Interpretation of subgroup findings should remain cautious. Apparent differences may reflect residual confounding, sparse data within categories, or multiple testing rather than true epidemiological contrasts. For this reason, subgroup analyses are best framed as hypothesis-generating unless they were defined a priori and supported by consistent patterns across complementary analyses. In reviews of S. mansoni prevalence, heterogeneity that persists after stratification should be explicitly reported, as it limits the certainty of pooled estimates and may justify presenting stratified summaries in preference to a single national prevalence value.

subsections.section_title: Systematic Review and Meta-Analytic Approaches to Synthesizing Prevalence Evidence
subsections.content:
Assessment of publication bias in prevalence meta-analysis should be interpreted cautiously because asymmetry in small-study effects may arise from genuine between-study heterogeneity, sparse data, or instability of variance estimates rather than selective publication alone. For studies of Schistosoma mansoni prevalence in Ethiopian children, visual inspection of funnel plots can be supplemented by formal tests such as Egger’s regression, but these results should be presented as exploratory rather than definitive, especially when the number of studies is small or when prevalence values cluster near 0 or 1, conditions under which conventional asymmetry tests perform poorly ref [56], ref [57].

Where asymmetry is suspected, reviewers should examine whether it is better explained by study features such as diagnostic method, region, sampling frame, or survey year before attributing it to publication bias. Sensitivity analysis is therefore essential: pooled prevalence can be re-estimated after excluding studies at high risk of bias, omitting statistical outliers, restricting to studies using comparable diagnostic procedures, or applying leave-one-out analyses to determine the influence of individual datasets on the summary estimate. Additional robustness checks may compare transformed versus untransformed prevalence models and fixed- versus random-effects assumptions to evaluate the stability of inference ref [57], ref [58].

In reporting, the review should distinguish clearly between evidence of small-study effects and confirmed publication bias, and should summarize how sensitivity analyses affect both the pooled prevalence and heterogeneity estimates. This is particularly important in parasitological surveys, where methodological diversity and geographically clustered transmission can generate substantial asymmetry independent of selective reporting.

subsections.section_title: Implications for Control Strategies, Policy, and Future Research
subsections.subsection_title: Preventive Chemotherapy and Mass Drug Administration
subsections.content:
Preventive chemotherapy with praziquantel remains the central short- to medium-term strategy for reducing schistosomiasis morbidity among Ethiopian children, particularly in settings where transmission persists through frequent water contact and limited sanitation. Programmatically, prevalence heterogeneity across districts argues for risk-stratified mass drug administration (MDA) rather than uniform scheduling. WHO guidance supports school-based treatment as the operational backbone in endemic areas, but Ethiopian control efforts should also account for non-enrolled children and preschool-age children who may be missed by routine delivery platforms and continue to contribute to the reservoir of infection ref [24].

For Ethiopia, the main policy implication is that MDA should be embedded within high-coverage child health and school systems, with explicit microplanning for hard-to-reach rural communities, pastoralist populations, and peri-water bodies where reinfection pressure is high. Evidence from multicountry analyses indicates that praziquantel substantially reduces prevalence and intensity in school-age populations, but repeated treatment is required because chemotherapy alone does not prevent rapid reinfection in persistent transmission settings ref [59]. This supports sustained annual or more frequent treatment in high-risk foci, alongside careful monitoring of therapeutic coverage, adherence, and post-treatment infection trends.

Future program refinement should therefore move beyond nominal drug distribution targets toward impact-oriented MDA metrics, including coverage among untreated subgroups, intensity reduction, and local rebound after treatment rounds. In Ethiopia, integrating MDA data with fine-scale endemicity mapping would help identify districts where treatment frequency can be safely reduced and those where intensified, combined interventions are necessary.

subsections.section_title: Implications for Control Strategies, Policy, and Future Research
subsections.content:
Water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) interventions are a necessary complement to preventive chemotherapy for schistosomiasis control among Ethiopian children because reinfection is sustained by frequent contact with cercaria-contaminated surface water during bathing, swimming, laundry, and water collection. For school-age populations, the most policy-relevant WASH priorities are reliable access to safe water, child-friendly sanitation in schools and households, and feasible measures that reduce direct contact with infested streams, ponds, and irrigation canals. Evidence from multi-country analyses indicates that improved water and sanitation access is generally associated with lower odds of schistosome infection, although effect sizes vary by setting and species, underscoring the need for locally tailored design rather than uniform prescriptions ref [60].

In Ethiopia, WASH programming should therefore be geographically targeted to transmission ecologies identified through prevalence mapping, especially lakeshore, riverine, and irrigation-linked communities. School-based platforms are particularly valuable because they can integrate safe water provision, latrine access, hand and body hygiene messaging, and practical risk reduction around recreational water contact. However, sanitation alone is unlikely to interrupt transmission where children continue to depend on unsafe water bodies for daily use. A broader intersectoral approach linking health, education, water authorities, and irrigation schemes is more consistent with current evidence that schistosomiasis control requires environmental improvements alongside chemotherapy and behavior change ref [61].

Future implementation research in Ethiopia should move beyond binary WASH indicators and evaluate intervention quality, functionality, use, seasonality, and distance to safe water points. Stronger study designs are needed to determine which combinations of infrastructure and behavior-focused interventions produce measurable reductions in child infection and reinfection in high-burden settings.

subsections.section_title: Implications for Control Strategies, Policy, and Future Research
subsections.subsection_title: Health Education and Behavior Change for Children and Communities
subsections.content:
Health education should be treated as a complementary, not ancillary, component of schistosomiasis control for Ethiopian children. Because reinfection is driven by repeated contact with infested water during play, bathing, laundry, and water collection, school- and community-based education can help translate prevalence evidence into locally relevant risk reduction. Experience from endemic settings indicates that knowledge gains alone are insufficient unless messages are practical, age-appropriate, and linked to feasible alternatives for daily water use and sanitation practices ref [62].

For children, curricula are likely to be most effective when delivered through schools, teachers, and peer-led activities, with simple emphasis on transmission pathways, symptoms, treatment benefits, and safer water-contact behaviors. For communities, behavior change efforts should engage caregivers, religious and community leaders, and local health extension structures so that messages address household decision-making and social norms rather than only individual awareness. Educational interventions are more credible when synchronized with praziquantel campaigns and with visible improvements in water access and sanitation, since integrated control has long been advocated as essential for sustainable reduction in schistosomiasis transmission ref [63].

Future Ethiopian programs should move beyond one-way information delivery toward behaviorally informed approaches that identify why children continue risky water contact despite treatment. Priority implementation research includes evaluating whether repeated school health education improves treatment uptake, reduces stigma or fear surrounding praziquantel, and shifts specific practices in high-transmission settings. Monitoring should therefore include intermediate outcomes such as knowledge retention, participation, and reported exposure behaviors, not only parasitological endpoints.

subsections.section_title: Implications for Control Strategies, Policy, and Future Research
subsections.content:
Effective schistosomiasis control in Ethiopian children requires surveillance systems that move beyond one-time prevalence estimates toward repeated, geographically explicit monitoring. Because transmission is highly focal and linked to water contact and snail habitats, district-level averages can mask persistent hotspots in schools and communities. National planning should therefore combine school-based parasitological surveys with finer-scale ecological risk mapping to guide treatment frequency, identify residual transmission foci, and prioritize integrated responses in high-risk settings ref [64].

Program monitoring should also account for the changing epidemiology expected under preventive chemotherapy. As prevalence declines, reliance on a single diagnostic approach may underestimate residual infection, especially light-intensity infections in children. WHO guidance on preventive chemotherapy underscores the need for regular impact assessment, treatment-coverage verification, and reclassification of implementation units based on updated infection data rather than historical endemicity alone ref [24]. In Ethiopia, this implies strengthening routine data quality, linking school and community surveillance, and building mechanisms to detect rebound after interruptions in mass drug administration.

Future surveillance strategies would benefit from integrating geospatial modelling, sentinel sites, and periodic independent coverage surveys. Such an approach can improve efficiency by concentrating resources where transmission persists, while also generating the evidence needed to shift from morbidity control toward interruption of transmission in selected settings.

subsections.section_title: Implications for Control Strategies, Policy, and Future Research
subsections.content:
Equity should be a central design principle for schistosomiasis control in Ethiopian children because infection risk is unevenly distributed across geography, livelihood, gendered roles, and access to services. Children in remote lakeshore, riverine, irrigation, and pastoral settings may be systematically missed by school-based delivery despite facing intense water contact and limited sanitation access. This implies that program success should not be judged only by average treatment coverage, but also by whether high-risk subgroups—including non-enrolled children, mobile populations, and communities with weak primary health infrastructure—are reached consistently.

Evidence from schistosomiasis control literature shows that preventive chemotherapy can leave important inequities unresolved when delivery platforms do not adequately capture non-school-attending children or socially marginalized groups ref [65]. More broadly, the WHO guideline on control and elimination emphasizes adapting interventions to local epidemiology and vulnerable populations rather than relying on uniform implementation assumptions ref [66]. In Ethiopia, this argues for combining school-based MDA with community-based outreach, locally tailored timing, and monitoring indicators disaggregated by sex, school attendance, district remoteness, and livelihood.

Equity considerations also extend beyond drug access. Communities with the highest transmission often face the greatest deficits in safe water, sanitation, transport, and diagnostic capacity, creating overlapping disadvantages that sustain reinfection. Future policy should therefore integrate schistosomiasis control with pro-poor WASH investment and stronger subnational surveillance, while research should examine who is persistently missed, why exclusion occurs, and which delivery strategies most effectively reduce inequities in endemic settings.

subsections.section_title: Implications for Control Strategies, Policy, and Future Research
subsections.content:
A major research priority is to move beyond single cross-sectional prevalence estimates toward longitudinal, age-stratified studies that capture reinfection, treatment response, and seasonal variation in transmission. In Ethiopian child populations, this would help distinguish persistent hotspots from transient high-prevalence settings and better identify the relative contribution of school attendance, water contact, sanitation access, and ecological factors to ongoing transmission. Methodologically, future studies should report diagnostic choice and sampling intensity transparently, because infection estimates vary substantially by test sensitivity, especially in low-intensity settings where reliance on a single stool or urine sample may underestimate burden.

A second gap concerns integration of parasitological, spatial, and implementation data. Geostatistical approaches have already shown that schistosomiasis risk is highly heterogeneous across environmental and community contexts, implying that district-level averages may be insufficient for child-focused control planning ref [67]. Linking prevalence surveys with treatment coverage records, school enrollment data, WASH indicators, and intermediate host snail surveillance would allow more precise targeting and more robust evaluation of why some areas respond poorly to preventive chemotherapy.

Finally, methodological priorities should include standardized reporting of diagnostic protocols, denominator definitions, and age categories to improve comparability across Ethiopian studies. Greater use of more sensitive assays alongside conventional microscopy may be particularly important as control programs reduce infection intensity; comparative work has shown notable differences in diagnostic performance between Kato-Katz and circulating cathodic antigen testing ref [68]. Implementation research is also needed to determine cost-effective combinations of school-based treatment, community outreach, and environmental interventions for hard-to-reach and persistently endemic child populations.
